See Abū Rayyān, the work cited above, p. 300.↩︎

On al-Suhrawardī’s trial, we can add another point that supports our interpretation of his position on prophecy. According to ʿImād al-Iṣfahānī’s account of al-Suhrawardī’s killing, the jurists who tried him accused him of stating in his writings that God was capable of creating a prophet after the Prophet Muḥammad. He did not deny the accusation. Instead, he limited his defense to proving that God had the power to do so. See Abū Rayyān, Uṣūl al-Falsafa al-Ishrāqiyya, pp. 17–18, and ʿImād al-Dīn al-Iṣfahānī, al-Bustān al-Jāmiʿ li-Tawārīkh al-Zamān, Claude Cahen ed., 1937–1938. If this account, found only in ʿImād al-Iṣfahānī, is correct, then it shows that al-Suhrawardī believed Muḥammad’s prophethood had come to an end. This position has another social and ideological meaning, because saying that Muḥammad’s prophethood had ended is one form of rejecting the ideological system on which the social and political order of the caliphate rested.↩︎

al-Suhrawardī explains the matter by saying that “anything whose existence depends on something else exists whenever that other thing exists.” He then applies this to the relation between God and the world: “The world is an effect of God, and God is eternal; therefore the world is eternal.” We have already stated that this follows from the impossibility of an effect lagging behind its cause. For that reason, “there can be no before or after in relation to the Light of Lights and what proceeds from it.” See Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, article 3, chapters 1 and 3.↩︎
Ibid. See also Abū Rayyān, Uṣūl al-Falsafa al-Ishrāqiyya, pp. 246–248.↩︎

We should note that al-Suhrawardī recognizes three “elements,” not four as in Aristotelian thought: earth, water, and air. Fire, in his system, is not an earthly element but belongs to the luminous world. Its “luminous” status is comparable to that of the soul, and he treats both as representatives of the higher light in the earthly world. The soul is the “greater representative,” while fire is the “lesser representative”: “God has a representative in every world.” Through the soul and fire, “the two representations, lesser and greater, are completed. This is why the Persians were once commanded to turn toward it”—meaning fire. See Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, pp. 422–423, 427–435.↩︎
Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq, article 3, chapter 1. al-Suhrawardī also argues for this thesis through the law of causality. See footnote 58.↩︎
See, for example, Qadrī Ḥāfiẓ Ṭūqān, al-ʿUlūm ʿinda al-ʿArab, Cairo, 1956, pp. 31–66.↩︎

He is Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn ʿArabī al-Ṭāʾī, named after the Arab tribe of Ṭayyiʾ. He was born in Murcia in al-Andalus in 560 AH/1164 CE. He lived there for about thirty-eight years and spent the rest of his life in the East. He died in Damascus in 638 AH/1240 CE. He was given the titles Muḥyī al-Dīn and “Sultan of the Knowers” because of his standing in Sufism and mystical knowledge. In the East he wrote some of the Sufi works in which he developed the idea of the “unity of being,” especially al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyya and Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam. He and Ibn Rushd lived at the same time and met in Córdoba. Ibn ʿArabī wrote a fascinating account of the meeting in al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyya, vol. 1, pp. 153–154, Cairo ed., 1329 AH.↩︎

One example of this rejection can be found in al-Sarrāj al-Ṭūsī, a fourth-century AH Sufi, who works hard to interpret every Sufi statement that seems to contain the idea of the “unity of being” in a way that removes that meaning. Examples include his interpretation of a statement on divine unity by Abū Bakr al-Shiblī (d. 334 AH/945 CE), and another statement on the same subject by Ruwaym al-Baghdādī (d. 303 AH/915 CE). See al-Ṭūsī, al-Lumaʿ, Cairo ed., 1960, pp. 50–51. Another example comes from al-Hujwīrī in the fifth AH/eleventh century, who describes Sufi fanāʾ as the annihilation of the servant’s will in God’s will, not the annihilation of the servant’s existence in God’s existence. See al-Hujwīrī, Kashf al-Maḥjūb, Nicholson’s English translation from Persian, Leiden, 1911, p. 245. al-Hujwīrī’s words clearly reject the idea of the unity of being.↩︎

In the Risālat al-Aḥadiyya attributed to Ibn ʿArabī, he says of knowing God: “...You must know Him not through knowledge, not through action, not through understanding, not through conception, not through sensation, not through perception...” See Three Muslim Sages, pp. 140–208.↩︎
The concepts of the Universal Intellect and the Idea are expressions of objective idealism. —Publisher.↩︎

The word “Adamic” in the title refers to Adam, whom the monotheistic religions call the father of humanity. Ibn ʿArabī, however, uses it to mean humanity as such; in the text, “Adam” refers to the human species, not simply to the individual Adam. The use of “word” may be influenced by the biblical idea “In the beginning was the Word,” where “word” expresses the will to bring something into being. The same idea appears in the Qurʾanic verse: “When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, ‘Be,’ and it is” (Qurʾan 2:117). Ibn ʿArabī’s use of “word” may also point to his idea that the world exists in two stages, as in the passage above: first as “an unpolished mirror,” then as a mirror that “required polishing.” If this is what he means, the title compares the world’s coming from God to a spoken word coming from a human speaker. A word also appears in two stages: first in an unclear form in the speaker’s mind, then openly in speech. In the same way, the world comes from God first as “a shape without spirit,” then as the open “manifestation” of the “most holy emanation.” See the passage above.↩︎
Ibn ʿArabī, ibid. See the previous page. All the phrases placed in quotation marks in this explanation are from the same source.↩︎

For Ibn ʿArabī, the term “greater human” means the whole world. When he uses “small world” or “smaller world,” he means the human being. These terms were used before Ibn ʿArabī, from at least the fourth AH/tenth century onward. We find them, for example, in the encyclopedia of the Brethren of Purity, Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, vol. 2, p. 213, and al-Risāla al-Jāmiʿa, vol. 1, pp. 582–587, vol. 2, pp. 26–27. But the Brethren used the terms differently: they meant that the structure of the world resembles the structure of the complete human body.↩︎

For Ibn ʿArabī, existence in itself is mercy. Everything that exists in the world exists because “the flow of divine existence through it is a mercy from God to it.” He uses “mercy” in this sense in Shajarat al-Kawn.↩︎

Chapter 27 of Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam is titled “A Singular Wisdom in a Muhammadan Word.” Ibn ʿArabī begins by explaining what makes this wisdom “singular” in relation to the “Muhammadan Word”: “His wisdom—that is, Muḥammad’s—was singular because he was the most perfect being in this human species. For this reason, the matter began with him and ended with him...”↩︎

This sentence comes directly after the words, “For this reason, the matter began with him and ended with him.” Together, the two statements indicate that the “Muhammadan Word” is the first existent being—that is, the first divine realization within the human species. We have already seen that the human being is the foundation of existence and the beginning of the link between God and the world. Muḥammad, then, is the first existent being in an absolute sense. Similar ideas appear in some Shiʿi sects in relation to Muḥammad, ʿAlī, and his family, as in the Tradition of the Cloak.↩︎

A clear picture of this reciprocal relationship between God and the human being appears in Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam, p. 104, where Ibn ʿArabī speaks of the purity of God’s shadow in the human being: “...This is a light extending from a shadow, and it is the very substance of glass. It is therefore a luminous shadow because of its purity. In the same way, in one of us who realizes the Truth [God], the form of the Truth appears more fully than it does in others. Among us are those for whom the Truth becomes his hearing, his sight, all his powers, and all his limbs, according to signs given by the revealed law that speaks of the Truth.”↩︎
ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn Ibrāhīm al-Jīlānī, or al-Jīlī (d. 832 AH/1428 CE).↩︎

As an example of what al-Jīlī says about the “Perfect Human,” we may cite the following: “...He—that is, the Perfect Human—is a copy of the Truth (...) God Most High is living, knowing, powerful, hearing, seeing, and speaking. The human being too is living, knowing, powerful, hearing, seeing, and speaking...” See al-Jīlī, al-Insān al-Kāmil fī Maʿrifat al-Awākhir wa-l-Awāʾil, Egypt ed., 1293 AH, vol. 2, p. 28.↩︎

In the first chapter of Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam, where Ibn ʿArabī lays out the foundations of the idea of the unity of being, he explains the status of the angels and the superiority of the human being over them. He says, for example: “The angels did not grasp what the formation of this vicegerent—that is, the human being—contained, nor did they grasp what the presence of the Truth requires in terms of worship rooted in the self. No one knows of the Truth except what his own nature allows him to know...” The angels do not possess “Adam’s comprehensiveness,” meaning the way the qualities of the whole cosmos come together in the human being.↩︎

In the history of Islamic sects and schools, we find figures such as Abū al-Khaṭṭāb Muḥammad ibn Abī Zaynab, whose followers first claimed that he was an “Imam” and then that he was a “prophet”; another man called Bazīgh; and a third called al-Sarī. The Manṣūriyya made similar claims for Abū Manṣūr al-ʿIjlī, an illiterate man. One branch of the Khaṭṭābiyya even took a man called ʿAmr as a god and worshipped him, while also believing in transmigration of souls, meaning their endless movement from one body to another. Examples of such sects are too numerous to count. See al-Nawbakhtī, Firaq al-Shīʿa, p. 38 ff., Istanbul ed., 1931; and al-Ashʿarī, Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn, vol. 1, p. 74 ff., ed.
